title: Restart Schedules for Ensembles of Problem Instances
unit: CPU time via a restart schedule (cutoff sequence)
items: ensemble of SAT instances (one schedule shared by all instances)
objective: minimize total/mean time to solve all instances
spread_rule: n/a (greedy on estimated per-instance run-length distributions)
evidence: Experiments: 'estimated mean CPU time increased by about 4% under leave-one-out'
notes: Greedy schedule from per-instance RTDs: 1.7x faster than Luby, 1.5x faster than best uniform (fixed-cutoff) schedule, 1.1x faster than best geometric. Main table evaluated on the same RTD estimates used to build it (in-sample), but the authors themselves report LOO cross-validation (+4%), so the E4 risk is acknowledged and quantified; not flagged E4. RTD estimation runs are offline (not charged). Heavy-tailed RTD on satisfiable formulae; non-heavy-tailed on UNSAT ones.

title: Combining Multiple Heuristics Online
items: heuristics/solvers interleaved; schedule shared across a set of instances
objective: minimize average time to solve instances
spread_rule: greedy: instances solved per unit time (4-approx)
evidence: Sec greedy algorithm: 'greedily maximize the number of instances solved per unit time'
notes: Offline greedy, learning-theoretic (train/test) bounds and a no-regret online version. Marginal-gain-per-cost greedy is exactly the 'marginal value' allocation for first-success objectives. Allocation is across solvers, not across instances, but the objective sums over instances.

title: Dynamic Restart Policies
items: runs on instances (each training run on a different instance), classified by observed solver-trace features
objective: minimize expected time to solution
spread_rule: n/a (cutoffs optimized per predicted run-time class)
evidence: Results: 'This shows the importance of pruning long runs'
notes: Clearest classical statement of 'do not spend on hopeless runs': runs predicted 'long' are pruned; 'naive' policy that gives each predicted class its own optimal cutoff performed poorly. 40-65% faster than Luby's fixed-optimal policy, ~6x faster than universal. Fresh test set. Observation window (10-1000 choice points) is part of the run, so charged. Pre-2010 classic.

title: Learning Dynamic Algorithm Portfolios (GambleTA)
venue: Annals of Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence
items: K algorithms run in parallel on each instance of an online instance sequence
objective: minimize total time to solve the sequence
spread_rule: quantile minimization of learned joint survival; mixed with uniform share via Exp4
evidence: Abstract: 'mixes the model-based shares with a uniform share'
notes: Uniform share is an explicit expert; model-based shares come from learned runtime distributions (survival analysis, censored sampling). Fully online, so the learning cost is paid in the evaluation itself. Items are algorithms, not instances.

title: Algorithm Selection as a Bandit Problem with Unbounded Losses
objective: minimize cumulative runtime (regret)
evidence: Abstract: 'algorithm selection as a bandit problem, with partial information, and an unknown bound on losses'
notes: Bandit over allocators (includes uniform). No item-level difficulty heuristic; neither E nor OK cleanly applies.

title: A Neural Network Model for Inter-problem Adaptive Online Time Allocation
items: multiple algorithms run in parallel on a sequence of tasks
objective: minimize time to solution over task sequence
evidence: Paraphrase (search snippet only): priorities updated by a neural model mapping state to expected time to solution.
notes: UNVERIFIED beyond snippet. GambleTA paper describes this predecessor as a 'ranking' heuristic, first problem with uniform share.

title: Learning Restart Strategies
items: sequence of instances (one restart strategy learned across the set)
objective: minimize total time to solve the instance sequence
spread_rule: bandit mix of Luby universal and estimated-optimal fixed cutoff
evidence: Secondary (Streeter et al. 2007): 'treats the schedule selection problem as a 2-armed bandit problem'
notes: Full text not retrieved; coded from two secondary descriptions (Streeter et al. 2007; Gagliolo & Schmidhuber 2006). Estimated-optimal cutoff = Luby's optimal fixed cutoff for the learned RTD.

title: Restart Strategy Selection Using Machine Learning Techniques
objective: number solved within cutoff and total runtime
evidence: Abstract: 'boost solver performance through a smart selection of the restart strategy'
notes: Per-instance choice among 9 restart strategies using SAT classifier + runtime models; 10-fold CV. Observation window precedes prediction (very easy instances solved before the window are omitted from the data). Selection, not a budget split; no flag.

title: SUNNY: a Lazy Portfolio Approach for Constraint Solving
unit: time slots within the per-instance timeout
objective: percentage solved / average solving time
spread_rule: time proportional to # k-NN neighbours each solver solves (+ backup slots)
evidence: Intro: time per solver 'proportional to the number of instances it solves'
notes: Direction: solvers more likely to succeed get more (easier-for-solver gets more), opposite of E2. A proportional rule spreads time thin; Lindauer et al. 2016 found Sunny 'tends to employ many algorithms per schedule' and capped it. 5x5 CV; feature-extraction time counted.

title: aspeed: Solver Scheduling via Answer Set Programming
items: solvers; one schedule applied to all instances
objective: minimize timeouts (then runtime) summed over instances
spread_rule: exact timeout-minimal schedule (ASP), L2-norm tie-break toward homogeneous slices
evidence: Abstract: 'non-uniform and ordered solver schedules from existing benchmarking data'
notes: Explicit comparison to the uniform ppfolio schedule; aspeed beat uniform in all cases, using 10-fold CV. Training runtime data are offline (not charged); authors study reduced training cutoff to cut that cost.

title: An Empirical Study of Per-Instance Algorithm Scheduling
objective: PAR10 on ASlib scenarios
spread_rule: ISA: timeout-minimal on k-NN neighbours; TSunny: proportional, capped size
evidence: Sec 4: 'Sunny tends to employ many algorithms per schedule'
notes: Hyperparameters (k, schedule size) chosen by CV on training data only. Finding: spreading time across too many solvers hurts; limiting schedule size helps.

title: Algorithm Selection and Scheduling
unit: runtime: static pre-solving schedule (~10% of budget) + selected solver
objective: number solved / PAR
evidence: Secondary (Lindauer et al. 2016): 'run the schedule for a small fraction of the runtime budget'
notes: Full text not retrieved; coded from Lindauer et al. 2016 description. Separation not verified -> no flag.

title: SATzilla: Portfolio-based Algorithm Selection for SAT
unit: runtime: pre-solvers with short cutoffs + selected solver
objective: instances solved / runtime
evidence: Secondary (Lindauer et al. 2016): 'SATzilla uses a grid search to obtain a pre-solving schedule'
notes: Pre-2010 classic. Feature computation time counted in SATzilla evaluations (from general knowledge, not re-verified here).

title: Continuous-Time Multi-Armed Bandits with Controlled Restarts
items: repeated tasks (SAT instances drawn from SATLIB set) under a total time horizon
objective: maximize expected total reward (problems solved) within a time budget
evidence: Fig. 3: 'gains on the number of problems solved per unit time'
notes: Restart rule: abandon a run when its residual reward rate falls below that of a fresh trial -- the marginal principle, cutting losses on long (hopeless) runs. Compared to Luby with several bases and no-restart.

title: The Potential of Restarts for ProbSAT
objective: expected runtime
spread_rule: optimal fixed cutoff from predicted RTD (Weibull etc.)
evidence: Abstract: 'Weibull distribution approximates the runtime distribution for over 93% of the used instances'
notes: Curve shape reported: Weibull RTDs. Per-instance cutoff from RF+NN predicted distribution; beats Luby and no-restart. Potential speedup 1.39 (empirical) / 1.30 (fitted).

title: LeapsAndBounds: A Method for Approximately Optimal Algorithm Configuration
objective: find configuration with near-optimal capped expected runtime using least total work
evidence: Abstract: 'tests configurations on randomly selected problem instances for longer and longer time'
notes: Budget across candidate configurations to identify the best = selection, not a sum over items.

title: Efficiency Through Procrastination: Approximately Optimal Algorithm Configuration with Runtime Guarantees
objective: find near-optimal configuration with worst-case runtime guarantees
evidence: Abstract: 'finds an algorithm configuration that provably achieves near optimal performance'
notes: Configuration selection; NA.
